articles.content_orig:
Top European diplomats will hold talks in Istanbul Friday with their counterparts from Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Egypt during a meeting initiated by Ankara, a Turkish foreign ministry source told the AFP news agency on Thursday.
Foreign ministers from the so-called E3 group – Britain, France and Germany – will meet counterparts from the newly created R4 group to discuss the Palestinian issue, developments in Yemen and the Strait of Hormuz and ways to end the Russia-Ukraine war, the source said.
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan will host the meeting, the first to bring together the two groups.
"The seven countries will come together for the first time in the R4+E3 format, at Turkey's initiative," the source said, indicating they would explore "opportunities for cooperation and coordination that could be put into practice ... in the coming period."
In chairing the meeting, Fidan was expected to focus on the international community "increasing pressure on Israel" in response to its settlement expansion and its "encouragement of settler terrorism," the source AFP.
Fidan will also underline support for Saudi Arabia's security in the face of attacks by Yemen's Houthis, and stress the need for permanent freedom of navigation in the Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb Straits.
Saudi Arabia's state-owned Saudi Aramco, the world's biggest oil company, told staff to evacuate the company's headquarters in the eastern city of Dhahran and to work remotely, the Reuters news agency reported Thursday, citing six sources with knowledge of the matter.
Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels have hit the kingdom repeatedly with missile and drone attacks in recent weeks.
Last week a missile struck an Aramco building in Dhahran, which is on Saudi Arabia's Persian Gulf coast. The strike caused a "limited fire" at Saudi Aramco's headquarters complex, the kingdom's energy ministry said at the time.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen's escalating civil war said Thursday that it had intercepted another drone over the Saudi capital Riyadh.
Coalition spokesman Maj. Gen. Turki Al-Maliki confirmed the interception in a social media post, without offering further details.
Saudi Arabia has been pummeled by Houthi strikes in recent weeks. Experts say geography, missile interceptor shortages and evolving Houthi tactics are helping the Iranian proxy menace the kingdom, and global energy supplies .
World shares and U.S. futures retreated Thursday as oil prices jumped more than 2% following a report by Iran's state television that seven oil tankers were hit by its military or sea mines and damaged near the Strait of Hormuz in the Persian Gulf.
If the claim by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps is verified, it would be the largest number of vessels damaged in the Gulf in a single day since the start of the Iran war on Feb. 28.
Brent crude, the international standard, gained 3.2% to hit $112.27 per barrel Thursday. It has been bouncing around $110 in recent days amid uncertainty about when the war with Iran might ease to allow the global energy shipments through the Strait of Hormuz to return to normal.
U.S. benchmark crude rose 2.8% to $99.80 per barrel.
In early European trading, Germany's DAX shed 1.1% to 25,367.96, while the CAC 40 in Paris declined 1.3% to 7,816.67. Britain's FTSE 100 was down 0.7% at 10,678.67.
The future for the S&P 500 lost 1% and that for the Dow Jones Industrial Average was 0.7% lower.
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said Thursday that it had struck four vessels transferring oil ship-to-ship in the Persian Gulf after they used a route through the Strait of Hormuz that Iran rejects. Ship-to-ship cargo transfers have become more common as tankers and other commercial vessels try to avoid Iranian detection and strikes in the strategic waterway.
In a statement, the IRGC Navy said it "monitored and pursued four violating vessels that had previously passed through an illegal route," referring to shipping lanes in the strait that the Trump administration has encouraged vessels to use to avoid Iranian fees and controls. Tehran considers those southern routes, close to Oman's coast, unauthorized and has targeted vessels trying to use them for months.
"They discovered the vessels transferring oil cargoes from ship to ship in the north-central part of the Persian Gulf," the bulletin read. "All four ships were hit simultaneously and are burning."
The IRGC said three other ships attempting to use routes not recognized by Iran "suffered accidents and caught fire after striking mines west of the Strait of Hormuz, and were brought to a halt."
The IRGC said the U.S. "encouraging vessels to pass through an illegally mined passage has led to an increasing number of maritime incidents day by day."
"If this course continues," the group warned, "the confrontation will extend to the bases of the aggressors in the region."
Saudi Arabia's civil aviation authority said Thursday that the latest attack on the kingdom's airports, a strike on the eastern city of Dammam's King Fahd International Airport, had risen to two.
"The number of deaths resulting from the attack has risen to two, after confirming an additional death. The deceased were a Saudi citizen and a resident of Indian nationality," the General Authority of Civil Aviation said in a statement shared on social media.
It said eight others, "a Saudi citizen, two residents each of Indian, Yemeni, and Bangladeshi nationalities, and a resident of Nepalese nationality," were injured in the attack.
The statement did not assign blame for the attack, but Iran's Houthi allies in Yemen have attacked Saudi airports and other infrastructure for weeks in retaliation for the Saudi government's backing of Yemeni state forces in the neighboring nation's decade-long civil war.
GACA said in its statement that it was continuing work in conjunction with other security authorities "to assess the damages, and to take all necessary measures to ensure the safety of passengers and employees, and to maintain the security and safety of the civil aviation system in the Kingdom."
Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia in recent weeks have inflicted severe losses on the kingdom and prompted the U.S. to quietly reduce its military footprint in the region as missiles hit energy infrastructure and civilian airports, killing more than 20 people.
Saudi Arabia, despite its size, wealth and a substantial military, has appeared to be on the back foot as it faces the Yemeni rebels.
Saudi Arabia spent $83 billion on defense last year, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute — far more than any other country in the Middle East , including Israel.
So, why has the kingdom struggled to stop the Houthi barrage? Read our full story here .
An attack targeting the King Fahd International Airport in the eastern Saudi Arabian city of Dammam killed one person and injured eight others Wednesday evening, the kingdom's civil aviation authority said.
The authority said in a statement that injuries from the attack ranged from "minor to serious" and that material damage to the airport was also being assessed.
It did not describe what type of attack occurred, but the kingdom's airports have been targeted repeatedly by projectiles in recent days by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi militants.
A U.S. official and a senior U.S. military official told CBS News on Wednesday the military has been quietly reducing its footprint at posts in the Middle East due to ongoing regional threats from the Houthis and direct threats from Iran.
NBC News was first to report on the drawdowns.
Asked about the reports, U.S. Central Command spokesperson Capt. Tim Hawkins told CBS News: "We regularly move U.S. service members and assets to optimize mission readiness. We do not discuss related movements for operational security reasons. U.S. forces remain vigilant and ready to protect American personnel and interests across the region."

articles.title_zh: Retired decorator's Pokémon cards sell for £1.5m
articles.content_orig:
Published: 06:33 EDT, 22 October 2026 | Updated: 07:29 EDT, 22 October 2026
A retired decorator has become a millionaire overnight after selling a haul of Pokémon cards he kept in his attic for a staggering £1.56million at auction.
The man, who wishes to remain anonymous, kept the collection in his home for 15 years - with no idea of their astonishing value.
After reading an article in his local newspaper about one Pokemon card selling for over £6,000, he decided to get his own assessed.
Cards from the Japanese cartoon franchise have reached cult status in recent years, with a spate of robberies across the country targeting shops selling packs.
Celebrities such as YouTuber Logan Paul have also helped drive the trend, with the American selling an ultra-rare card for $16million (£12million) this year.
In the latest example of the items drawing in an incredible amount of cash, the retired decorator from Woking in Surrey, took a sample of his attic collection to Ewbank's Auctions in nearby Guildford.
The auctioneers' jaws 'hit the floor' when they laid eyes on the 42 sets of collectibles - 'all in mint condition' - and they estimated initially that the cards could fetch up to £270,000.
Head of Ewbank's auctioneers Andrew Ewbank (pictured, left) and head of trading cards James Spooner (pictured, right) pose with the cards which sold for a staggering £1.56million
Some of the cards included in the retired decorator's collection, which had been in his attic
But the collection soared past that guide price at auction on Wednesday, as YouTubers, collectors and investors bid up to £100,000 for a single lot.
James Spooner, head of trading cards at Ewbank's, said: 'When we saw what he had - all in mint condition - we couldn't believe it, or the fact that he had no idea what they were worth.
'When we then discovered that he had 42 such sets, our jaws hit the floor. We got to sell 41 of them, and he kept one.
'This is easily the most valuable collection we have handled so far - we thought it might go as high as £270,000, then the pre-sale bids started coming in and we realised we were on to something much bigger.
'The day before the sale, we already had £825,000 in commission bids.'
Titled Pokémon: A Decade of Masters (1999-2009), the single-owner collection proved to be the auction house's most successful sale in over 30 years in business.
Do YOU think Pokémon cards are now a serious investment?
The top lot in the collection was the Legendary Collection Complete Master Set, which featured all 110 cards, the 110 Reverse Holo 'Firework' cards and the four Box Toppers
Titled Pokémon: A Decade of Masters (1999-2009), the single-owner collection proved to be Ewbank auction house's most successful sale in over 30 years in business
The top lot was the Legendary Collection Complete Master Set, which featured all 110 cards, the 110 Reverse Holo 'Firework' cards and the four Box Toppers.
With the vital Charizard in near-mint condition, it had been pitched at between £15,000 and £20,000 - but went for a hammer price of £100,000.
The collector says he bought the cards relatively cheaply in the 1990s - with one set he purchased for £300 selling for £75,000 at auction.
He said: 'When my son was young, in the late 1990s, he started getting cards and swapping them at school. I thought they looked nice and wondered whether they might be a good investment.
'I was lucky enough to find someone in Malaysia who sold complete sets, and I bought a couple of things from them on eBay.
'They then asked me if I would be interested in buying a complete master set of Pokemon cards, as they had about two or three master sets for each issue.
American YouTuber Logan Paul sold his PSA 10 Pikachu Illustrator for $16.492million at auction in February, setting a Guinness World Record for the most expensive trading card ever sold
'I thought that it would be cheaper to buy the full set rather than keep buying sealed packs of random cards in hope that when you opened them you could complete a set.
'The first set I bought cost me around £300. It's the Sky Ridge Charizard set.'
The cards, which were all carefully inserted in the bespoke Pokemon binders while still sealed and in mint condition, had been stored in the attic after the owner's son lost interest.
The collector added: 'He had his own cards, but he never got to touch these, I'm glad to say.
'I know people always talk about finding treasure in the attic, but in my case that is literally true. I had no idea what I had until the team at Ewbank's explained it to me.'
At the end of the auction, Andrew Ewbank - who runs the business set up by his late father Chris and conducted the sale from the rostrum himself - thanked bidders and told them he was 'going for a lie down'.
Later, he said: 'The build-up to this sale has been phenomenal, and on the day it did not disappoint. We had bidders from all over the world and more bidders in the saleroom itself at any time since before the Covid pandemic.
'The buzz was incredible, especially because the collectors could not believe how good this collection was - extensive, untouched, complete and with just about every rarity you could hope for.'
Pokemon cards were first released in Japan in October 1996, based on the franchise's video games, before arriving in North America and Europe in 1999.
The cards were designed to let fans collect their favourite characters while also building decks and battling against one another, helping turn to it into a social collecting and gaming hobby.
The cards have become a serious investment market and must-sell item, with rare Pokémon cards steadily increasing in value and continuing to command eye-watering prices at auctions globally.
American YouTuber Logan Paul sold his PSA 10 Pikachu Illustrator for $16.492million (roughly £12.32million) at auction in February, setting a Guinness World Record for the most expensive trading card ever sold at auction.
Paul, a YouTuber-turned-WWE star, had acquired the card in 2021 for $5.275million (roughly £3.94million), meaning its latest sale price was more than three times that figure.
Their surging value has also made them a new target of thieves, with a spree of burglaries for the cards 'more valuable than gold' happening at collectible and gaming shops across the country.

articles.title_orig: Barclays to Cut 5,000 Jobs in AI-Fueled Push to Lower Costs
articles.title_zh: Barclays to Cut 5,000 Jobs in AI-Fueled Push to Lower Costs
articles.content_orig:
By ANGHARAD CARRICK, BUSINESS NEWS EDITOR and PATRICK TOOHER, CONSULTANT CITY EDITOR
Updated: 07:16 EDT, 22 October 2026
Barclays will cut 5,000 jobs by the end of this year as it pushes to replace staff with artificial intelligence.
The lender, which reported another profit surge last quarter, said there had already been 1,000 roles axed, with a further 4,000 planned by the end of the fourth quarter.
The job losses form part of a growing shift in the banking sector towards the technology in a bid to cut costs.
Earlier this month, HSBC was reported to have been readying for a 'brutal' jobs cull in its wealth management division.
Barclays, which is nearing the end of a three-year cost-cutting drive, said the cuts would prune 5 per cent of its workforce.
‘We employ AI at scale but AI is the icing on the cake, it is not the cake,’ Barclays chief executive CS Venkatakrishnan, who is known as Venkat, told analysts.
Barclays expects to make ‘efficiency savings’ of at least £1.1billion next year with Venkat vowing he would ‘drive hard’ at realising more gains from adopting AI.
It is unclear how many of the 5,000 full-time job cuts will be in the UK, but 3,000 of them will be in ‘support’ roles, including software developers.
Barclays CEO CS Venkatakrishnan said AI had been the 'icing on the cake'
Venkat highlighted how technology had reduced online mortgage application times from 45 minutes to 15 minutes and meant ten percent fewer staff were needed in each bank branch.
‘These little things go a long way,’ he added.
It came as the lender reported another boost in profits in the third quarter, with plans to hand out more cash to investors ahead of a tax raid on banks in next week’s Budget .
Barclays posted a 12 per cent rise in pre-tax profits to £2.3billion for the three months to September 30, compared to £2.1billion a year earlier.
But the results were overshadowed by the looming windfall tax on bank profits in John Healey’s first Budget as Chancellor on Wednesday.
The biggest banks, including Barclays, pay a 3 per cent surcharge above the 25 per cent corporation tax rate.
This is expected to increase to 8 per cent under Healey’s plans to bring in an extra £2billion a year to the Treasury.
Industry figures have warned it will hit investment and growth, pushing up mortgage rates in the process.
Barclays boss CS Venkatakrishnan has previously pleaded with the Treasury to leave the bank levy at its current level, telling reporters that ‘for every £1 of capital we have, we lend £8 to £10’ to businesses and households that supports economic growth.
This morning, Barclays also revealed plans for a new £500million share buyback, bringing distributions so far this year to £2.8billion, up 46 per cent year-on-year.
Paul Nowak, general secretary of the Trade Union Congress, said: ‘Barclays’ bumper profits aren’t an anomaly.
'All the big banks are doing exceptionally well at the same time – but their windfall profits have been underpinned by mortgage misery for millions. That’s why it’s time for banks to pay a fairer share.
‘At a time when the chancellor needs to raise more revenue to support households and businesses through a looming energy bill crunch, Britain’s big four banks have made £200bn in profit since 2021. They can – and should – pay more tax.’
Banks’ profits have been boosted in recent years because of higher-for-longer interest rates , which have widened the gap between what they pay savers on deposits and charge borrowers for lending.
This gap – net interest income – is a key measure of profitability for lenders. For Barclays UK, it rose 6 per cent year-on-year to £2billion in the third quarter as the fallout from the Middle East war pushed interest rate expectations higher.
Income from both its UK retail and corporate banks increased, as well as from the wealth management arm and investment arm.
The investment bank, which makes up around 48 per cent of revenues, generated £3.1billion, boosted by trading volatility.
Income from equities soared 47 per cent to £689million as traders continued to take advantage of market volatility caused by the war in the Middle East as well as the latest moves in AI stocks.
Barclays' share price, which has suffered since news of the Chancellor’s tax plans, fell 2 per cent in early trading.
Venkatakrishnan said he was ‘pleased with the ongoing momentum of Barclays’ operational and financial performance’.
John Healey declared banks a 'jewel in the crown of the British economy' and now he's looking to tap them for additional revenue.
Targeting the financial sector with higher levies comes with trade-offs, with concerns over the UK's competitiveness and its knock-on impact on economic growth.
Any increase to the banking surcharge could be passed on to consumers through higher mortgage rates and other loans, trade body UK Finance warned last month.
To protect their profit margins, domestic banks could raise their mortgage prices or offer less competitive rates on new deals.
A higher surcharge may limit flexibility and therefore lead to tighter lending criteria, making it more difficult for prospective buyers to secure a mortgage approval.
Savers could also be punished. Lenders may cut interest rates on savings accounts to try to recoup the lost revenue caused by higher taxes. Lower rates while inflation is rising means reduced real returns for savers.
Meanwhile, those who rely on dividend income from UK banks may also take a hit after the Budget if banks reduce shareholder payouts to cover the tax bill.

articles.content_orig:
China's benchmark CSI 300 index on Thursday entered bear-market territory, falling 20% from its June peak, as a prolonged sell-off in its equities deepens.
The index, which tracks 300 of the largest stocks listed in Shanghai and Shenzhen, has declined for 10 consecutive weeks and is down 2.6% so far this week, underscoring sustained pressure on Chinese equities, data from LSEG showed. The index was more than 1% lower Thursday.
Jordan Cvetanovski, chairman and CIO at Pella Funds, said China's equity market continues to face structural challenges, particularly as the world's second-largest economy grapples with the fallout from years of excess capacity and overinvestment.
"I think China is really struggling with reining in the problems that they've had in the past from the overbuild of capacity and other things," Cvetanovski told CNBC, pointing to challenges facing companies even in globally competitive industries such as batteries — a sector where he still sees select opportunities in China.
Chinese firms have been suffering from declining profit growth amid intense competition that has eroded margins and even invited the government to step in. In September, the country posted it's weakest growth in industrial profits this year.
The world's second-largest economy also posted its slowest growth in over three years in the second quarter, pressured by a multiyear slowdown in the property sector and extended weakness in consumer demand.
Shaun Rein, managing director at China Market Research Group, expects further selling pressure as geopolitical uncertainty, concerns over an artificial intelligence bubble and deteriorating consumer confidence weigh on investor sentiment.
China's large base of retail investors could also exacerbate market volatility, Rein said, as individual investors are prone to exiting the market faster during periods of uncertainty.
Unlike major markets such as the New York Stock Exchange, where retail investors account for about 20%-25% of trade volumes, China's retail investors drive 90% of daily trading, according to data provided by HSBC.
"For Chinese, it's about wealth preservation," Rein said, noting that investors are increasingly favoring safer assets such as time deposits amid a weakening property market and sluggish labor conditions.
While Rein expects increased pressure on markets, he said the sell-off has been excessive, pointing to resilient exports and signs of a recovery in property prices in China's largest cities.
"It's a crisis of confidence right now not a crisis in the economy," he said, predicting a strong rebound in Chinese equities in 2027.
Daniel Gerard, senior multi-asset strategist at State Street Markets, also struck a more optimistic tone, saying that China's growing capabilities in artificial intelligence could eventually draw global investors back into its equity market, even before corporate earnings recover.

articles.title_orig: How do Israel's elections work and who are the main contenders?
articles.title_zh: How do Israel's elections work and who are the main contenders?
articles.content_orig:
Israel's general election takes place on Tuesday 27 October.
It's the first election since the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attacks on Israel and its subsequent conflicts in Gaza and with Iran, Hezbollah and the Houthis.
Many view it as one of the most pivotal elections in Israel's history, with global implications.
Current polling puts incumbent Benjamin Netanyahu in a tight race with Gadi Eisenkot, a former head of the Israel Defense Forces, to become prime minister.
Eisenkot's popularity stems partly from his military credentials and his relative newness in politics, having formed his Yashar Party only last year.
He lost his son, a soldier, in the first months of the Gaza war, and served in Israel's war cabinet under Netanyahu until resigning in 2024 over disagreements about the conflict. He has built his campaign on calls for accountability over the security failures that led to 7 October.
Other opposition leaders include former prime minister Naftali Bennett and Avigdor Lieberman - both right-wingers who take hardline positions on security and advocate permanent Israeli control over much of the occupied West Bank - and Yair Golan, a left-winger who supports Israel's withdrawal from large parts of the territory. Despite their differences, they could work with Eisenkot to form a government.
Netanyahu's current government is the most right-wing in Israel's history. In order to remain in power, he will likely have to rely on the support of some of his existing far-right coalition partners. Some hold ultra-nationalist positions, such as calling for Israel to annex the West Bank and for the "migration" of Palestinians from Gaza - which could amount to the forced displacement of civilians. Some members of Netanyahu's own Likud party have also called for Palestinian "migration" from the territory.
There are two Arab party blocs in the running too, as about one-fifth of Israel's population is Arab - many of whom describe themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel. In theory, they could prove kingmakers. But all but one of the leading Jewish parties have ruled out working with them.
Israel's parliament - known as the Knesset - has 120 seats, meaning a government must hold 61 seats to command a majority.
Israel uses a proportional representation voting system, meaning governments have always been coalitions of multiple parties.
This means that after election day, it may take weeks or even months before the next government is formed - with different parties wrangling for concessions and deals being struck.
If no bloc can form a majority, it is possible a minority government could take power.
The dominating topic has been security - with the challengers to Netanyahu all heavily criticising the security failures that led to the 7 October attacks, in which nearly 1,200 people were killed and 251 others taken back to Gaza as hostages. Nevertheless, Netanyahu has once again framed himself as "Mr Security", pointing to strategic victories in Israel's wars since 2023.
Conscription is also a major topic. Historically, ultra-Orthodox Jewish men in full-time religious study have been exempt from military service, but since war broke out this has become an increasingly divisive policy.
Judicial reform has also featured heavily during the campaign. Netanyahu's government is still pursuing contentious plans for reforms to the judicial system, which led to mass protests before 7 October. Critics say the plans would compromise the independence of the judiciary and threaten democracy.
As in many countries, cost of living is another key issue. Food and housing costs have grown steadily in recent years.
A year on from the ceasefire in Gaza, Israel continues to carry out near-daily strikes on the territory - saying it is targeting Hamas operatives - and maintains control of more than half of it.
More than 74,000 people have been killed in Israeli attacks on Gaza since 7 October 2023, according to the Hamas-run health ministry - whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
In the West Bank, attacks by Jewish settlers are at an all-time high, according to UN records, while Israeli settlements, which are illegal under international law, are rapidly expanding.
So for Palestinians, the shape of Israel's government is a major factor in their lives.
On Gaza, the two leading camps - headed by Netanyahu and Eisenkot - hold similar positions - with both supporting Donald Trump's peace plan, which would see Hamas give up its weapons in exchange for a phased Israeli troop withdrawal from the territory. Eisenkot recently pledged to end Hamas rule in the territory within 18 months, through military means if necessary.
In the West Bank, Netanyahu's camp largely wants to continue with its policy of settlement expansion.
Eisenkot supports Israeli settlements in general, but opposes proceeding with the controversial E1 settlement project which would, in effect, split the West Bank in two. He also wants to close some unauthorised settler outposts built on Palestinian land, create conditions for a final peace settlement with the Palestinians, and crack down on extremist Jewish settlers.
For decades, many mainstream Israeli politicians advocated for a two-state solution - the creation of an independent Palestinian state in peaceful coexistence alongside Israel - although Netanyahu has long opposed it. But support for the idea has been declining for years. In this election, none of the leading Jewish parties are campaigning on it, and many have outright rejected it.
At 22:00 local time (20:00 GMT) on election day, Israeli broadcasters will publish exit polls. These will give some indication of the direction of voting, but can vary significantly and current polling suggests a clear projected winner is unlikely.
Preliminary results are expected the next day, with official results scheduled to be published on 4 November.
After consulting with party leaders, President Isaac Herzog will then invite whichever leader he believes has the best chance of forming a government to do so.
This process can take more than a month, and if it fails the president may ask another leader to try. If that also fails, Knesset members can ask the president to allow a third leader to try. And if that fails, new elections will be called.
Between 2019 and 2022, Israel held five separate elections as parties struggled time and again to co-operate.

articles.title_orig: Elon Musk Met Xi Jinping and Took Tesla FSD to China — Now His CFO Says Getting the Green Light for Unsup
articles.title_zh: Elon Musk Met Xi Jinping and Took Tesla FSD to China — Now His CFO Says Getting the Green Light for Unsup
articles.content_orig:
The logo of Tesla is displayed on a smartphone screen with the SpaceX logo in the background.
The world’s richest man has publicly backed a potential combination of SpaceX and Tesla in what could be the biggest merger in history.
On Tuesday, Elon Musk , the CEO and largest shareholder of both companies, said the electric vehicle maker and the rocket company had formed special committees at the request of shareholders to discuss the idea.
“I do think there’s a lot of merit to combining the companies as we are pretty much in the superintelligence singularity, ​and there’s a lot to be gained from cooperating,” Musk told SpaceX investors on a conference call.
“I think it would be a good ​idea, but it’s really up to the special committees of both companies,” he added.
The committees, which are made up of independent directors, would need to agree on the transaction terms of any deal before putting it to shareholders for a vote. Musk said his conflict of interest prevents him from participating in their discussions.
Musk has previously teased a Tesla-SpaceX merger. On a July 22 earnings call, Musk said there was “more and more overlap” between Tesla and SpaceX as the companies expand into artificial intelligence and robotics. Last week, Barclays analysts suggested that a merger could be announced before Tesla’s annual shareholder meeting in December.
Tuesday’s call was the first confirmation that the companies were formally exploring a combination.
A merger could create a company worth around $3.5 trillion , putting it among the world’s most valuable companies. It could also become the biggest merger ever by deal value, potentially surpassing SpaceX’s record-setting $250 billion acquisition of Musk-owned AI company xAI in February. SpaceX is currently valued at about $2 trillion, and Tesla at $1.5 trillion. A deal could also help propel Musk back into trillionaire ranks , depending on its terms and how investors value the combined company. Musk owns around 48% of SpaceX and 20% of Tesla.
The shares of both companies rose in after-hours trading on Tuesday. SpaceX, which went public in June, reported a quarterly net profit of $4.4 billion. Musk told investors he expects annual recurring revenue of between $500 billion and $1 trillion by the end of 2027.
Some analysts, however, have warned of regulatory and geopolitical hurdles, particularly in terms of Tesla’s Chinese operations and SpaceX’s U.S. defence work. Morningstar analysts said a merger could raise U.S. national security concerns involving the combined company’s supply chain. JPMorgan analysts also flagged regulatory approval in China as a potential stumbling block.
Any deal could also face congressional scrutiny, which could intensify if Democrats win control of either chamber in the coming midterm elections. Democratic lawmakers have previously questioned Musk over conflicts of interest and raised national security concerns about reported Chinese investments in SpaceX. Democrats have also challenged major acquisitions in the past on consumer protection grounds. In June, Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D, Mass.) criticized SpaceX’s IPO, citing Musk’s concentrated voting power and weak investor protections—concerns that could resurface in a Tesla-SpaceX merger.
A merger could bring two of Musk’s biggest businesses under one corporate umbrella, making it easier for the companies to move investments and resources between projects. “This would allow him to run all their operations under one roof without tripping on as many governance issues,” wrote Morningstar analysts Seth Goldstein and Nicolas Owens in June. “For example, Musk could move Tesla software developers or engineers to work on SpaceX AI projects, and vice versa, or have Tesla and SpaceX supply one another without the need for related party transaction disclosures or risking shareholder lawsuits claiming the resources of one firm are being diverted for the benefit of the other.”
Analysts noted that Tesla’s robotaxis could benefit from Starlink connectivity, while its autonomous vehicles and Optimus humanoid robots could more closely integrate SpaceX’s AI technology. SpaceX’s planned orbital data centers, meanwhile, could potentially benefit from access to Tesla’s battery and energy storage products.
A combined company could also mean greater control of several stages of the AI value chain, from chip design and planned manufacturing to computing infrastructure, AI software, and its deployment in vehicles and robots.
The companies already collaborate. In March, they announced Terafab , a joint semiconductor manufacturing project intended to produce chips for Tesla’s vehicles and humanoid robots and SpaceX’s planned AI satellites. SpaceX technologies have also been used in some Tesla products, including the new Roadster prototype , which uses SpaceX-developed thrusters.
David Nicholson, chief technology advisor at market research firm The Futurum Group, told the BBC that a merger also appears to align with Musk’s long-held ambition of colonizing Mars . Musk previously outlined plans to send Tesla’s Optimus robots to the planet aboard SpaceX’s Starship spacecraft.
A merger could also strengthen Musk’s influence over Tesla’s direction. Barclays estimated that a SpaceX acquisition of Tesla could give Musk around 37% of the combined company while controlling around 56% of its voting power. He currently controls around 82% of voting power at SpaceX and 20% at Tesla . That could represent either a benefit or a risk for shareholders, as decision-making would become faster but have fewer checks.
“One thing I don’t think people talk enough about with SpaceX and Tesla as well: You do still have a huge amount of key-man risk here,” wrote Morningstar analyst David Sekera earlier this month. “God forbid anything were to happen to Elon Musk.”

articles.title_orig: Russia Pounds Kyiv in Overnight Missile and Drone Barrage – 1 Dead, 24 Injured, Including 4 Children
articles.title_zh: Russia Pounds Kyiv in Overnight Missile and Drone Barrage – 1 Dead, 24 Injured, Including 4 Children
articles.content_orig:
In brief: Russian ballistic missile and drone attacks on Kyiv killed one person and injured 24 others, including 4 children. Strikes damaged metro infrastructure on the South Bridge, an ambulance station, six emergency vehicles, homes and businesses.
Russian forces launched successive waves of ballistic missiles and attack drones against Kyiv overnight into Thursday, Oct. 22, killing one and injuring at least 24 people, including four children, and damaging a metro bridge, an ambulance station, residential buildings and civilian infrastructure across the Ukrainian capital.
Initially, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko reported in a Telegram update Thursday morning that the number of injured had risen from six to 15, including two 15-year-old children.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
However, the State Emergency Service (DSNS) reported at 7:55 a.m. that one person had been killed and 22 others injured, including four children, in Russian attacks on the capital.
In a statement issued at 9:21 a.m., the Kyiv City Military Administration said that 24 people had been injured, 16 of whom had been hospitalized.
Russian forces launched ballistic missile strikes on six districts of Kyiv starting on the evening of Oct. 21, causing fires and damage, the DSNS said:
Dniprovskyi district: One person was killed, and a child was hospitalized. Homes and vehicles were damaged, while residential and non-residential buildings caught fire. Five other people were injured.
Darnytskyi district: Transport infrastructure was damaged. No injuries were reported.
Sviatoshynskyi district: A non-residential building and a restaurant complex caught fire. The blaze, which covered 1,100 square meters, has been extinguished.
Obolonskyi district: Non-residential buildings were damaged, and fires broke out. Two people were injured. The fires have been extinguished.
Pecherskyi district: Buildings, ambulances and a monastery were damaged. Eight people were injured, including three children.
Holosiivskyi district: Six people were injured when a non-residential building was struck.
The overnight bombardment also damaged metro infrastructure on Kyiv’s  South (Pivdennyi) Bridge, prompting traffic restrictions on a key crossing over the Dnipro River.
In the central Pecherskyi district, Russian strikes damaged an ambulance station and six emergency medical vehicles, according to the mayor.
The latest attack marks another assault on essential civilian infrastructure in Kyiv, with Russian missiles hitting residential neighborhoods, transport facilities and emergency medical services.
The Russian bombardment also struck part of the capital’s metro infrastructure on the South Bridge, a major crossing connecting Kyiv’s two banks.
“As a result of the shelling, part of the metro infrastructure on the South Bridge was damaged,” Klitschko reported on Telegram .
The Kyiv City Military Administration announced traffic restrictions on the bridge in the direction from the right bank to the left bank because of the attack.
The bridge carries both road traffic and a section of Kyiv’s green metro line across the Dnipro.
Damage to the crossing adds pressure to Kyiv’s transport network as the capital faces repeated Russian attacks on civilian infrastructure.
Russian strikes also damaged an emergency medical facility in Kyiv’s Pecherskyi district.
Klitschko confirmed that the damaged building was an ambulance station and that six ambulances had also sustained damage.
No medical personnel were injured, the mayor said.
The damage to emergency medical services came as ambulances and rescue crews were responding to casualties elsewhere in the capital.
The overnight strikes also sparked a fire at a restaurant building in Kyiv’s Sviatoshynskyi district.
The Kyiv City Military Administration reported that the fire broke out following the Russian attack, adding another civilian site to the growing list of damaged properties.
Earlier Wednesday evening, Russian missiles struck residential buildings and businesses in Dniprovskyi district.
Klitschko reported direct hits on a vehicle repair workshop and a private residential building, while debris damaged another house.
Emergency crews were dispatched amid concerns that people could be trapped beneath the rubble.
At another location in the same district, missile debris fell near a gas station, causing additional damage.
In Darnytskyi district, a Russian strike hit the grounds of a transport infrastructure facility, according to the mayor.
Ukraine’s Air Force issued repeated warnings as Russian ballistic missiles approached the capital late Wednesday and after midnight Thursday.
The warnings began during Wednesday evening’s assault, when explosions were reported across Kyiv.
Further ballistic missile threats followed after midnight, including warnings shortly after 12 a.m. and another at approximately 12:31 a.m.
The Air Force also tracked Russian attack drones approaching the Kyiv region and subsequently warned of a drone over the capital.
The successive threats forced residents to remain in shelters as emergency crews responded to damage across multiple districts.
Russian forces launched a massive combined missile and drone attack against Ukraine beginning at 6 p.m. on Oct. 21, targeting Kyiv as the primary strike location, the Ukrainian Air Force reported.
The attack involved Iskander-M and S-400 missiles, Zircon and Oniks missiles, and 210 strike drones, including jet-powered Shahed-type drones, Gerbera and Italmas drones, and Parodiya (Parody) decoy drones.
“The primary target of the strike was Kyiv,” the report said.
The attack was countered by Ukrainian Air Force aircraft, anti-aircraft missile units, electronic warfare (EW) and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of Ukraine’s Defense Forces.
As of 9 a.m. on Thursday, preliminary data showed that Ukrainian air defenses had shot down or suppressed 181 Russian drones, including 87 jet-powered Shahed-type drones, Gerbera drones and other types.
“Ten strike drones remain in the air; combat operations are ongoing! Do not ignore air raid alerts!” the Air Force warned at 9.01 a.m.
Russian weapons struck 32 locations, while debris from intercepted drones fell at eight other locations.
The latest strikes came amid renewed US-led diplomatic efforts to negotiate an end to Russia’s war against Ukraine.
On Wednesday, US special envoy Steve Witkoff met Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg after holding discussions with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and European officials earlier in the week.
The Kremlin subsequently signaled willingness to resume trilateral negotiations involving Ukraine, Russia and the US.
However, Moscow has not abandoned its territorial claims or its opposition to Ukraine joining NATO.
Meanwhile, Russian forces continue attacking Ukrainian cities and essential infrastructure as winter approaches.
Ukrainian officials have repeatedly stressed that any negotiated settlement must include reliable security guarantees to prevent renewed Russian aggression.

articles.title_orig: 5 simple ways to relieve the aches and pains of sitting at a desk all day
articles.title_zh: 5 simple ways to relieve the aches and pains of sitting at a desk all day
articles.content_orig:
Back pain, eye strain, sluggishness, shoulder aches, restlessness.
If you sit in front of a computer for long periods of time, whether it's for work or leisure, you've probably experienced one of these symptoms.
But there are ways to relieve some of this discomfort — and even combat some of the health risks that may come with prolonged sitting. That includes walking breaks, ergonomic solutions and quick, simple stretches.
Here's a roundup of tips that have been previously featured on Life Kit.
We know that a sedentary lifestyle isn't great for human health. Studies have shown it can lead to fatigue, weight gain and back and joint pain — and it's been linked to chronic diseases like obesity, heart disease and cancer. Yet adults in the United States spend an average of 9.5 hours sitting per day, involved in activities tied to computers, laptops and phones.
But there may be a way to mitigate its harms. In 2023, researchers at Columbia University Medical Center set out to find the least amount of movement you need to counteract the dangers of prolonged sitting. And they found that walking for five minutes every 30 minutes was the most effective strategy .
In 2023, our colleagues at NPR's Body Electric tested out this five-minute walking exercise on our NPR listeners. Over 20,000 participants joined the challenge — and reported higher productivity and lower fatigue .
Want to give this walking challenge a try? Get instructions from Body Electric — and use this worksheet to keep track of your walking breaks .
Anyone who works at a desk knows how easy it can be to slip into a slouch. If we're not careful, that mid-back rounding can creep into all of our sitting time and create pain by putting stress on the middle section of our spine.
This movement above seeks to relieve that stress and encourage flexibility by mimicking the natural movements of the spine — side bending, bending backward and rotating, says Vinh Pham, a physical therapist. The idea is to get the body comfortable with these motions so that when you encounter them in real life, they're not painful.
To do this modified movement, which Pham calls the 3D T-spine rotation, stand up and drop your right foot behind the left, about a foot apart. Starting with the right arm straight up and the left arm behind you, as if you're shaking the hand of the person behind you, simultaneously drop your arms — still in a straight position — and twist toward your right foot. Move them back to their original position and hold for two seconds. Repeat the movement ten times before switching legs and doing the same exercise on the other side.
For more pain-relieving stretches, read this story.
When you stare at a screen for long periods of time, your eyes have to work hard. They must first turn inward to look at a close subject, then adjust the focus for short vision and hold that position.
Digital eye strain, as eye doctors call it, can cause eye fatigue, headaches or blurry vision. Try the exercise below to relieve that strain.
Fidgeting is a sign you need to break out of a stagnant posture, says Katy Bowman , a biomechanist and author of Rethink Your Position and Movement Matters . Even a position that feels comfortable at first can begin causing back pain, headaches or stiffness if you hold it long enough .
So listen to your body and mix things up. Alternate between sitting, standing, reclining and moving. That might mean opting to stand in the back of a conference room during a big staff meeting, taking a call while going on a walk or reading a report with your feet propped up in the break room.
The goal is to put yourself in configurations that contort your body in different ways. They should be "adaptive and dynamic" and easy to "change in and out of," says Leada Malek , a physical therapist and author of the book Science of Stretch.
Don't worry too much about what is "good" and "bad" posture. Both Malek and Bowman agree on a common phrase among physical therapists: "Your best posture is your next posture."
Your monitor screen should be at eye level so you're not craning your head down to see. And, your keyboard and mouse should be low enough so you're not shrugging your shoulders and lifting up your arms like a praying mantis to type and click.
Meg Honan, a professional ergonomist, says this common "head down and arms up" position sets you up to feel "achy, sore and tired." To combat this uncomfortable and oftentimes painful position, try repositioning your tech. Bring your laptop or desktop monitor screen up to eye level with a stack of books or some other platform.
Place your keyboard and mouse at a lower height where you don't have to shrug your shoulders to use them. If your keyboard is attached to your laptop, consider connecting an external keyboard and mouse so you can have the computer screen at your eye level and lower your arms. External mouses don't just help lower our arms, but they also prevent the constant strain of using a trackpad.
For more ergonomic tips, read our story .

articles.title_zh: Attack on Saudi Arabia’s King Fahd airport kills two people
articles.content_orig:
Saudi Arabia’s General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA) said in a statement on Thursday that the number of people killed in an attack on King Fahd International Airport in the eastern city of Dammam has risen to two – a Saudi national and an Indian resident.
The GACA also said the attack which took place on Wednesday left eight people wounded.
Earlier in the day, two people were killed after Saudi air defences intercepted a drone that was attempting to hit a facility at Saudi Aramco’s Shaybah oilfield, the Ministry of Energy said.
It was the latest in a series of assaults on Saudi infrastructure as conflict intensifies between Houthi forces and the Saudi-backed internationally recognised Yemeni government.
Last week, the kingdom reported that a projectile strike on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport on October 11 killed one person and injured 11. On October 10, the civil aviation authority reported that a separate attack on the same airport claimed the lives of 12 people and injured more than 300.
On Wednesday, the US State Department ordered diplomats and family members to depart from its missions in Saudi Arabia amid the ongoing Houthi attacks. There are also plans to withdraw family members from a number of other US missions in the region, US officials told Reuters.
The US embassy in Riyadh issued a security alert on Wednesday about possible further attacks by the Houthis on Saudi Arabia.

articles.title_orig: Stocks Slide as AI Trade Falters and Oil Rallies: Markets Wrap
articles.title_zh: Stocks Slide as AI Trade Falters and Oil Rallies: Markets Wrap
articles.content_orig:
U.S. equity futures slid on Thursday, bogged down by declines in mega-cap names Meta Platforms and Tesla along with a jump in oil prices as geopolitical tensions rise.
Dow Jones Industrial Average futures lost 356 points, or 0.7%. S&P 500 futures fell 1%, and Nasdaq-100 futures dropped 1.7%.
Tesla shares dropped more than 3%, while Meta slipped nearly 2%. The declines came even after the former's third-quarter results beat estimates — though its automotive revenue was lackluster — while the latter exceeded revenue expectations and offered upbeat guidance.
Technology more broadly was under pressure as well as ongoing concerns about artificial intelligence spending persisted. Advanced Micro Devices fell more than 4%, while Micron Technology and Nvidia dropped 3% and 2%, respectively.
Additionally, neocloud CoreWeave, whose bond yields and credit default swaps remain elevated , declined nearly 4%. The move comes as Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told CNBC Thursday that demand for neoclouds is " off the charts ." However, he added that capital is scarce and impeding growth.
JPMorgan traders noted that Wednesday's bullish "tone reversed overnight" because Meta shares rolled over in the premarket and chatter increased "over renewed Iran kinetic-risk post US mid-term election."
Additionally, "underlying price actions and feedback from our trading desk also suggested the still fragile narrative around AI financing concerns and the lack of conviction/re-grossing from the recent tech reversal," they said in a note to clients.
Oil prices, meanwhile, jumped more than 2% after The New York Times reported, citing sources, that the U.S. and Israel have plans for renewed strikes against Iran following next month's midterm U.S. elections. Brent crude traded 2.7% higher at $111.77 per barrel. WTI advanced 2% to $99.25 per barrel.
Investors also turned to U.S. Treasurys in their search for a safe haven. The benchmark 10-year Treasury note yield dropped 7 basis points to 5.069%. The 2-year note yield also shed 6 basis points to trade at 4.761%.
The action follows a positive day on Wall Street, with the S&P 500 notching a three-day win streak.
Looking ahead to Thursday, there are a host of companies on deck to report results including Procter & Gamble, Lockheed Martin, Valero Energy and Honeywell.
Investors will also be paying attention to the economic calendar with weekly initial jobless claims set to release Thursday morning.
Europe's Stoxx 600 index was down 1% in morning deals, while France's CAC 40 index fell 1.34%.
South Korea's Kospi fell more than 1%, while Japan's Nikkei 225 declined 0.73%. Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index was down more than 2%. Mainland China's CSI 300 was down 0.37%.
Spotify Technology delivered a slight miss on both operating income and revenue compared to expectations in its third-quarter earnings report, according to FactSet.
However, forecasts for operating income for the fourth quarter came in above estimates, and U.S.-listed shares of the Swedish company were higher in premarket trading Thursday. The stock was rising more than 5% before the bell.
The company also reported 306 million subscribers, slightly above estimates for 305.11 million, according to StreetAccount.
"We've built a strong business that keeps compounding, we invest when we see a path for growth, our costs are moderating, and there is more runway ahead," Spotify co-CEO Alex Norström said in a statement about the results.
Oil prices surged Thursday after The New York Times reported, citing sources, that the U.S. and Israel have plans for renewed strikes against Iran following next month's midterm U.S. elections.
Brent crude traded 2.7% higher at $111.77 per barrel. WTI advanced 2% to $99.25 per barrel.
Birkin bag designer Hermès dropped to the bottom of the Stoxx600 index after reporting third-quarter earnings highlighting a drop in demand from Chinese consumers.
The French luxury brand saw total revenue for the third quarter rise 4.3% to 4.1 billion euros ($4.6 billion), recording growth in America, Japan and Europe. However, sales of its ready-to-wear and accessories division as well as watches fell during the quarter. It also flagged that growth in the Middle East and France was slightly down.
Hermès was last down nearly 7%.
"Back to China now, what we see is that it's the volume divisions that are suffering, so fashion accessories, for example, and also watches and shoes," Chief Financial Officer Eric du Halgouet ⁠said in the earnings call.
"It has to do with a drop in footfall that we have been able to offset with greater value, which is the strength of Hermès. With other divisions like jewelry, leather goods, and such, it's really a matter of footfall more than anything else, and the volume-related mid-tier that suffers the most."
Halgouet ⁠also emphasized that regarding recent protests in Paris, the brand has "reinforced security and safety" of its staff and stores, but it's too early to gauge the impact on the business and on tourism.
Asian stocks tumbled on Thursday, led by a sell-off in technology shares.
The MSCI All Country Asia Pacific ex-Japan Index fell over 2% to its lowest level in nearly three months, putting it on course for a fourth consecutive weekly decline.
Japan's Nikkei 225 reversed earlier gains to decline 2.6% to 62,907.84, while the Topix lost 1.1% to 3,997.5.
South Korea's benchmark Kospi was down 3.52% to 5,533.77, while the small-cap Kosdaq was down 3.6% at 764.1.
China's CSI 300 index shed 1.8% to 4,036.30, while Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index declined 3% in its last hour of trade.
Many technology names were seen lower in early premarket, with Intel and Marvell Technology both down more than 5%, Micron Technology down 3.5% and Qualcomm down 2.94%.
Nvidia shares were seen 2.2% lower.
French borrowing costs remained under pressure in morning European deals Thursday, with the yield on the 10-year OAT up nearly 6 basis points to 5.0514%.
The yield closed Wednesday around 5.02% , its highest level since 2002.
Mass protests and rioting over the weekend have further spooked investors , compounding existing concerns that the country's politicians will struggle to pass reforms to reduce the budget deficit and tackle its growing debt .
French stocks on the CAC 40 index were down 1.33% in early trade. Luxury goods giant Hermes fell 6.3% after missing analyst expectations for third-quarter revenues.
The pan-European Stoxx 600 was down 0.78% shortly after 8:10 a.m. in London (3:10 a.m. E.T.) as the continent's main bourses and sectors started Thursday's session mainly in the red.
Basic resources shed 2.22%, leading losses, as travel and leisure stocks slumped 1.94% in early dealmaking. Banks slipped 1.93% while technology names were down 1.79%.
Food and beverage stocks advanced more than 1%, while telecoms rose 0.39%, and oil and gas ticked 0.14% higher.
The French CAC 40 shed 0.82% in Paris, while Italy's FTSE MIB dropped 0.96% in Milan. In Frankfurt, Germany's DAX opened 0.73% lower, while in London, the U.K.'s FTSE 100 futures slipped 0.54%.
Nestlé CEO Philipp Navratil told CNBC Thursday that while third-quarter results were strong globally, the U.S. has been a tough market as shoppers face budget strains and seek value.
"Look, the U.S. numbers were also good in Q3... but consumers are still cautious, so it's not an easy environment in the U.S. at all," Navratil told CNBC's Carolin Roth on "Squawk Box Europe."
"Consumers look for value, they are stretched at the end of the month, and so we have to adapt the portfolio to the right price points," he said.

"We anticipated the enemy's actions and mastered the tactics of conducting combat operations underground," he said.

articles.title_orig: China's Stock Market Crashes 20%: 3 Reasons Why The Dragon Is Losing Its Fire
articles.title_zh: China's Stock Market Crashes 20%: 3 Reasons Why The Dragon Is Losing Its Fire
articles.content_orig:
China's benchmark CSI 300 index on Thursday entered bear-market territory, falling 20% from its June peak, as a prolonged sell-off in its equities deepens.
The index, which tracks 300 of the largest stocks listed in Shanghai and Shenzhen, has declined for 10 consecutive weeks and is down 2.6% so far this week, underscoring sustained pressure on Chinese equities, data from LSEG showed. The index was more than 1% lower Thursday.
Jordan Cvetanovski, chairman and CIO at Pella Funds, said China's equity market continues to face structural challenges, particularly as the world's second-largest economy grapples with the fallout from years of excess capacity and overinvestment.
"I think China is really struggling with reining in the problems that they've had in the past from the overbuild of capacity and other things," Cvetanovski told CNBC, pointing to challenges facing companies even in globally competitive industries such as batteries — a sector where he still sees select opportunities in China.
Chinese firms have been suffering from declining profit growth amid intense competition that has eroded margins and even invited the government to step in. In September, the country posted it's weakest growth in industrial profits this year.
The world's second-largest economy also posted its slowest growth in over three years in the second quarter, pressured by a multiyear slowdown in the property sector and extended weakness in consumer demand.
Shaun Rein, managing director at China Market Research Group, expects further selling pressure as geopolitical uncertainty, concerns over an artificial intelligence bubble and deteriorating consumer confidence weigh on investor sentiment.
China's large base of retail investors could also exacerbate market volatility, Rein said, as individual investors are prone to exiting the market faster during periods of uncertainty.
Unlike major markets such as the New York Stock Exchange, where retail investors account for about 20%-25% of trade volumes, China's retail investors drive 90% of daily trading, according to data provided by HSBC.
"For Chinese, it's about wealth preservation," Rein said, noting that investors are increasingly favoring safer assets such as time deposits amid a weakening property market and sluggish labor conditions.
While Rein expects increased pressure on markets, he said the sell-off has been excessive, pointing to resilient exports and signs of a recovery in property prices in China's largest cities.
"It's a crisis of confidence right now not a crisis in the economy," he said, predicting a strong rebound in Chinese equities in 2027.
Daniel Gerard, senior multi-asset strategist at State Street Markets, also struck a more optimistic tone, saying that China's growing capabilities in artificial intelligence could eventually draw global investors back into its equity market, even before corporate earnings recover.

articles.title_orig: World's largest wealth fund posts $30 billion loss after bond market turbulence
articles.title_zh: World's largest wealth fund posts $30 billion loss after bond market turbulence
articles.content_orig:
Norway's sovereign wealth fund — the largest in the world — said Thursday that its investment portfolio delivered a loss of $30 billion in the third quarter, as rising interest rates dented returns on its bond holdings.
Norges Bank Investment Management (NBIM), which manages the $2.3 trillion fund, said the accounting return for the period was a loss of 278 billion kroner ($29.7 billion). Around 70% of NBIM's fixed income portfolio is allocated to government bonds, with the remainder invested in corporate debt.
The third quarter saw a global bond market rout . Government bond yields surged as major central banks, including the U.S. Federal Reserve, began rate-hiking cycles and concerns about inflation and government debt levels mounted.
NBIM's fixed income investments delivered a negative return of 3.5%, with the fund's management saying this was a key driver of the overall downturn.
"The fund's return was close to flat, ending slightly negative as rising interest rates led to weaker results on our fixed-income investments," NBIM's Deputy CEO Trond Grande said in a statement.
Fixed income accounts for just over a quarter of the fund's entire portfolio, with NBIM invested in 1,664 bonds across 51 countries.
Last month, NBIM said it wanted to cut its U.S. Treasury holdings as part of wider plans to reduce its allocation to government-issued debt.
Equities, which account for 72% of the sovereign wealth fund's investments, returned 0.5% for the fund in the third quarter.
The fund has small stakes in around 7,100 companies across most countries. With holdings in 1.5% of all listed companies globally, it is the world's largest single investor.
Stock markets were turbulent in the three months to September. Wall Street's major averages ended the third quarter in mixed territory. The S&P 500 index added 2.03%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 1.9% and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite ended the quarter 2.2% higher.
The average change across the three indexes was just 0.6%, marking a slowdown in the rally that saw double-digit gains in the previous quarter.
NBIM is an investor in America's biggest companies, with its top holdings including a $65.4 billion stake in Nvidia , as well as positions in Apple , Alphabet and Microsoft .
Its positions in the world's biggest companies make NBIM influential in terms of both voting power and setting investment trends.
"Equity returns were also close to zero, but there were large differences between sectors. Energy companies rose the most, while interest-rate-sensitive sectors such as utilities and real estate fell," Grande said Thursday.
Energy stocks benefited from surging oil prices in the third quarter, as the U.S.-Iran war continued, said NBIM, which has stakes in various energy majors, including Exxon Mobil , Shell and Chevron .
Over the summer, NBIM CEO Nicolai Tangen told CNBC that investors should not expect a continuation of the bumper gains seen in the stock market in the first half of this year.
"For sure, we should not be expecting the same kind of returns going forward as we've seen over the last six months," he said at the time.
The fund delivered a first-half return of 12.95%, and a record first-half profit nearing $185 billion. It also invests in real estate and renewable energy infrastructure, which returned 0.4% and 7.5%, respectively, in the third quarter.
Norway established its sovereign wealth fund in 1998 to invest revenues from the country's oil.

"Gen Z regelt" — or Gen Z's Got It — a youth initiative, has called for mass protests in 21 cities across Germany on Saturday, October 31; including Berlin, Cologne, Hamburg and Munich.
Thousands are expected to participate in demonstrations protesting "broken schools and austerity," as well as the cost of living, social injustice, military conscription and climate change.
French protests that exploded in violence and rampant destruction of private and public property this weekend also grew out of student frustration over the national school system and soon included numerous unions , groups and individuals voicing anger over a number of issues.
Gen Z regelt's website clearly states that the initiative is "against all violence," whether directed at people or property.
Police say they are "vigilant and relaxed," adding that they intend to protect people's right to congregate and express their opinions.
Still, images of massive damage and public violence from France , Italy and Spain have raised concerns among domestic policymakers and police, who have warned against allowing the protests to be hijacked by left-wing extremists.
Andreas Roßkopf, head of the German Federal Police's GdP union, made clear that officers would deal harshly with riots and rioters, telling the Rheinische Post newspaper on Wednesday, "state, but also federal police, will offer a firm and decisive response" to any trouble.
Roßkopf also warned that radicals and extremists could insert themselves among demonstrators in order to "attack police" or "simply be destructive."

Adelaide Zoo recorded its first Southern Cassowary egg in 34 years.
Ten-year-old Martina laid the bright green egg after being paired with 13-year-old Jeffrey.
The egg's fertility is unknown, and incubation takes about 50 days.
Adelaide Zoo in Australia celebrated the arrival of its first cassowary eggs in decades.
Two cassowary eggs were laid over the last few days, according to the zoo's Facebook page.
The milestone comes after caretakers carefully paired the zoo's female cassowary, 10-year-old Martina, with its 13-year-old male, Jeffrey, for the first time.
FILE - One of two cassowary eggs that were laid at Adelaide Zoo. (Zoos SA via Storyful)
Zoo employees have yet to confirm whether the eggs are even fertilized, but the fact that the eggs were laid at all is still a huge success for the species, according to a zoo news release.
"This is really exciting news for us because it has been 34 years since we've had successful cassowary chicks here at Adelaide Zoo, so the team and myself included are very excited," Team Supervisor Birds and Free Flight, Erin, said.
Since it is unclear whether the eggs have been fertilized, caretakers will be monitoring the nesting area and the birds' behavior closely in the meantime.
Cassowary can lay a clutch of between three and five eggs, according to the zoo.
It takes about 50 days to incubate and typically the male cassowary cares for and raises the chicks.
The bright green color of the shell helps camouflage the eggs from predators, according to the zoo.

articles.title_orig: Beatings, cyberattacks and threats darken Vucic's Serbia ahead of elections
articles.title_zh: Beatings, cyberattacks and threats darken Vucic's Serbia ahead of elections
articles.content_orig:
Unorthodox campaign is challenging the ruling party’s 14-year reign with a bold democratic experiment
O n a cool autumn evening, a team of Serbian student volunteers went canvassing in the housing estates of Krnjača, a Belgrade suburb. They were equipped with lanyards emblazoned with the word “victory”, a stock list of questions and a mobile app that mapped visited homes and the level of support in each.
The volunteers were part of a mass student movement, Student List, that has rocked Serbia with two years of constant protests. On Sunday, the group will represent the most serious challenge Aleksandar Vučić has faced in his 12 increasingly authoritarian years in power, by putting forward their own candidates in parliamentary elections.
They hope to emulate the defeat of Vučić’s ally, Viktor Orbán , in neighbouring Hungary six months ago, in a domino effect that could bring a democratic resurgence to central Europe.
Opinion polls have varied wildly, but many expert observers say a close race is quite possible, with neither side prepared to accept a loss as a legitimate result, raising the risk of post-election unrest and clashes.
In order to win, the students’ list of 250 candidates would have to break the mould of Serbian politics, along with Vučić’s grip on the country. He stepped down as president last month, five months before the end of his second and last term in office under the constitution, but only with the aim of extending his hold on power as prime minister at the head of his Serbian Progressive party (SNS).
In the section of the suburb assigned to them, law student Zak Veličković and campaign photographer Danijela Radojković were welcomed with overwhelming support. Apart from a small handful of polite doorstep rejections, from those claiming they had no interest in politics, people seized the opportunity to air their grievances.
Most promised their vote and a large minority offered help: some taxi drivers with flats in the low-rise apartment blocks said they would help ferry voters to the polling stations.
“Turnout is the key,” one said, adding: “Orbán fell with 80%” – a reference to the Hungarian elections in April .
Veličković began each conversation by asking what was the biggest problem in Serbian society, a query that often raised a laugh and replies such as: “How much time do you have?”
Corruption was the most frequent single complaint. On the corruption index run by Transparency International , Serbia ranks far worse than any of its neighbours, as the most corrupt country in Europe bar the dictatorships in Belarus and Russia.
There are frequent allegations of links between the SNS and organised crime, and the Student List’s slogan confronts that widespread perception head on, posing the question: “Serbia or Mafia?” The government denies all accusations and officially claims to be tackling organised crime.
The key local issues in Krnjača were the poor repair of the road bridge linking the suburb and central Belgrade, and the sewage system, which repeatedly fails in heavy rain, despite a personal promise by Vučić, who residents said had visited a few years earlier, to fix the problem.
The economy has been growing in recent years, but there is a widespread opinion that the fruits are not being fairly distributed. Porsche and Land Rover car showrooms have been established in Krnjača but public spaces look neglected. Some of Belgrade’s trams are more than 50 years old.
It was a major infrastructure failure that sparked the student protests – the collapse of a concrete canopy in Novi Sad railway station on 1 November 2024, killing 16 people. Evidence pointed to botched modifications made during refurbishment work, but so far there has been no official finding on the cause, and no official has been held accountable.
When Belgrade students blocked a road in a vigil for the victims three weeks after the disaster, they were attacked by a SNS mob and the protest movement went nationwide.
The students initially distanced themselves from opposition parties and avoided any kind of hierarchy or conventional leadership structure. That was partly an ideological choice and partly practical. The SNS and state-run media rule in part through smearing opponents and the student’s collective approach offered fewer targets.
Vučić rose to prominence in the 1990s as a radical nationalist, who supported the policies of Serbian expansion and ethnic cleansing led by Slobodan Milošević, who died of a heart attack in detention in The Hague during his trial on charges of genocide and crimes against humanity committed in Croatia, Bosnia and Kosovo. He served as Milošević’s information minister throughout the Kosovo conflict. As president, Vučić has not emulated his predecessor’s militarism, but he has maintained his nationalist playbook in domestic politics, dismissing the opposition as stooges of unspecified foreign powers.
So far those well-worn tactics have proved ineffective against the students. A survey published in July by a Serbian pro-democracy group, the Centre for Research, Transparency and Accountability (CRTA) and Stanford University showed significantly more support for the students (45%) than for the SNS (36%), but that was well before Vučić announced his resignation on 27 September and his election machine went into top gear. Other, more recent domestic polls show the SNS in the lead, though the pollsters in question are seen by the opposition as pro-government.
Vučić himself shows signs he is taking the political threat seriously enough to throw himself into the campaign, making 129 live television appearances in August, more than four times the previous month’s total.
“Serbia has been an electoral autocracy and in electoral autocracies only ruling political parties can win,” Raša Nedeljkov, CRTA’s programme director, said. But he added that the status quo was now in jeopardy.
“What we are seeing in the past days, weeks, months, is that strength; the homogeneous government that Vučić used to have is no longer there. He is faced with a completely unorthodox political actor and the toolbox that he has improved over the years since he came to power is no longer effective.”
Unable to crush the students by force, division or denigration, Vučić gambled, announcing his resignation as president and calling snap elections, in the apparent hope of catching the students off guard, but they responded by improvising a democratic experiment.
The 250 candidates were mostly nominated by university faculties (there are more than 160 doctorates among them) with a sprinkling of farmers and other professions, and each candidate was subject to approval by plenary sessions of the student protests.
after newsletter promotion
The policy platform has also been decided by plenum, with the result that divisive issues, especially foreign policy, have been played down: the question of future EU membership has been left to a referendum and Kosovo is claimed as an integral part of Serbia.
One of the chosen candidates, Milica Jovanović, an assistant professor at the University of Belgrade, argued the List’s lack of political experience was not necessarily a drawback.
“We are political amateurs, but we are experts,” Jovanović said. “We are people who have led projects, led organisations, led our community, and actually I cannot see that we can do worse than these politicians … The only thing that matters is willingness to improve something, expertise to actually do it and support to do the actual change.”
The Student List is pitted against the political monolith of the SNS, in power for 14 years and with control of the state apparatus. It has accused the foreign ministry of rigging the diaspora vote by keeping polling stations open where support for Vučić is strong, such as the Serbian part of Bosnia, while closing them in parts of North America where the opposition could expect to perform well. The ministry did not respond to a request to comment.

El Salvador has initiated a military operation to rescue four Salvadoran soldiers abducted by gangs in Haiti, President Nayib Bukele announced in a post on X, without elaborating.
Bukele, known for his intense crackdown on gang violence in El Salvador, warned in Wednesday’s statement that a more forceful response was coming if the personnel were not released alive and well.
“Do not take our word for empty threats,” the president wrote, addressing the gangs allegedly responsible for holding the four men. “We have already finished with the gangs in El Salvador, and we can finish with you too.”
Gangs in Haiti opened fire on an armoured vehicle carrying the men three days earlier, in the first major attack since an international gang suppression force began operating in the violence-wracked Caribbean country last year.
The four men, aviation technicians with the United Nations-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF), have been missing since they fled the burning vehicle in the Santo area of Croix-des-Bouquets, Port-au-Prince.
Haiti’s government issued a news release on Wednesday evening saying the release of the abducted soldiers was an “absolute priority”.
It was not immediately clear if Haitian authorities received any confirmation that the Salvadoran soldiers are alive.
The government said a meeting was held at the prime minister’s office “to assess the ongoing interventions and determine the necessary measures to strengthen operations, in close collaboration with the Gang Repression Force”.
A spokesperson for the GSF did not immediately respond to a message seeking details
The UN-backed force is still fighting gangs in the community where Sunday’s attack occurred, warning residents in the area to remain indoors.
No one has claimed responsibility for the attack on the Salvadoran troops, which comes as Haiti prepares for its first general election in more than a decade. It also showcases the power of the gangs that control an estimated 70 percent of the capital, Port-au-Prince.
El Salvador is among several countries – including Chad, Jamaica and Guatemala – to form part of the gang suppression force, with more than 2,000 troops on the ground in Haiti.
Gang violence has displaced nearly 1.5 million people in Haiti in recent years. More than 5,700 people have been killed or injured from January through mid-September this year, and more than 230 have been kidnapped, according to the UN.
